facts.text: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 meters (72 feet) on each side.
Gold is weighed in troy ounces. A troy ounce is about 31.1 grams, a little heavier than the everyday ounce of 28.35 grams.
The first gold and silver coins were made by the kingdom of Lydia (in today's Turkey) around 2,600 years ago.
In 1933 the U.S. government made it illegal for most people to own gold coins, bars or certificates. The ban lasted until 1974.
For about a century the U.S. dollar was defined as a weight of gold: $20.67 an ounce until 1934, when it was reset to $35.
On August 15, 1971 President Nixon ended the dollar's link to gold. That closed the Bretton Woods system and let currencies float.
Gold first crossed $1,000 an ounce in March 2008 and first crossed $2,000 an ounce in August 2020.
Fort Knox is said to hold about 147 million troy ounces of U.S. gold, roughly 4,580 tonnes.
The California Gold Rush started in January 1848 when James Marshall spotted gold at Sutter's Mill. About 300,000 people came for it.
The Klondike Gold Rush (1896 to 1899) pulled tens of thousands of prospectors north to Canada's Yukon.
In 2022 and again in 2023, central banks bought more than 1,000 tonnes of gold in a year, the most in decades.
Pure gold is soft enough to shape by hand, which is why jewelry gold is mixed with other metals. 24 karat means pure.
Vikings paid in silver by weight. They cut up coins and jewelry into pieces called hacksilver and weighed them on small folding scales.
Tens of thousands of Arabic silver coins have been dug up in Scandinavia, proof that Viking traders reached the Islamic world.
Viking trade ran from Greenland in the west to Constantinople and the Caspian Sea in the east, using rivers like the Volga and the Dnieper.
Hedeby, in today's northern Germany, was one of the biggest Viking trading towns. Its mint was among the first in Scandinavia, around the 820s.
In 845 the Franks paid a Viking fleet 7,000 pounds of silver to leave Paris. Paying off raiders with silver became known as Danegeld.
Arm rings of silver and gold were money, status and pay all in one. Poets called a generous king a ring-giver.
The Scandinavian coin names ore and oyri (Danish, Norwegian, Swedish and Icelandic) go back to the Old Norse eyrir, an ounce of silver.
Norse sailors reached North America about 1,000 years ago. Their camp at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland has been dated to the year 1021.
Erik the Red settled Greenland around the year 985.
Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, is one of the oldest parliaments still around.
Dublin began as a Viking settlement in the 840s, and Viking Dublin struck Ireland's first coins around 995.
Viking longships were light and shallow, so crews could sail across open sea and then row up rivers deep into a country.
There is no evidence Vikings wore horned helmets. The idea comes from costumes made for an 1876 opera.
Thursday is Thor's day and Wednesday is Odin's day (Woden's day). Our weekday names carry the old Norse gods.
Most Vikings were farmers and traders. Raiding was only part of the story, and the Viking Age is usually dated from the 793 attack on Lindisfarne to 1066.
King Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the early 1000s, an empire around the North Sea that linked trade across the whole region.
The word Viking comes from the Old Norse vikingr. To go a viking meant to go on an overseas expedition for trade or plunder.
The Cuerdale Hoard, found in England in 1840, held about 8,600 pieces of Viking-age silver weighing around 40 kilograms.
Much of the Arabic silver in Viking hoards was minted in Central Asia, in cities like Samarkand and Tashkent, thousands of miles from Scandinavia.
A Norwegian silver penny from the 1000s turned up at a Native American site in Maine. It was probably carried there by trade.
A small Indian Buddha statue from around the 500s was dug up at Helgo, Sweden, a sign of how far Viking-age trade reached.
Some Viking swords carry the name Ulfberht on the blade. A number of them were made of unusually pure steel for their time.
In 865 a large Viking army landed in East Anglia and fought across England for years. The English called it the Great Heathen Army.
King Alfred of Wessex beat the Viking leader Guthrum at Edington in 878. Afterward much of eastern England became the Danelaw, under Danish law.
Place names ending in -by or -thorpe in England, like Grimsby and Whitby, mark where Norse settlers lived.
In 911 the Frankish king gave the Viking leader Rollo land around the river Seine. It became Normandy, the land of the North men.
William the Conqueror, who won England in 1066, was a descendant of the Viking Rollo.
Harald Hardrada, the last great Viking king, was killed at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in England on September 25, 1066.
From about 988 the Byzantine emperor guarded himself with the Varangian Guard, an elite force with many Norse warriors.
The name Russia may come from the Rus, the name given to the Norse traders who sailed down the rivers of eastern Europe.
In 922 the Arab traveler Ibn Fadlan met Norse traders on the Volga River and wrote down what he saw, one of the best eyewitness accounts of them.
More than 2,000 runestones survive in Sweden alone. Many were raised to remember a family member who died.
The Oseberg ship, buried in Norway in 834 and dug up in 1904, is one of the best-kept Viking ships ever found.
Five Viking ships were sunk on purpose around 1070 to block a Danish fjord. They were raised in 1962 and rebuilt.
In 1893 a copy of the Gokstad Viking ship crossed the Atlantic in 44 days on its way to the Chicago World's Fair.
Small silver Thor's hammer pendants have been found across the Viking world, much like people wear a cross today.
A famous Viking grave at Birka in Sweden was long assumed to hold a male warrior. DNA tests in 2017 showed the person was a woman.
The Icelandic word for Saturday, laugardagur, means washing day. The Vikings are known for being clean, with combs and tweezers in many graves.
English borrowed words from the Vikings, including sky, egg, knife, window, husband, law and skull.
The Bluetooth logo is made from the runes of the initials of Harald Bluetooth, a Danish Viking-age king who united Denmark.
Norse settlers began making homes in Iceland around the year 874.
Berserker may mean bear shirt, a warrior who fought in a frenzy. Some scholars think it means bare shirt, with no armor.
Viking navigators used the sun, stars, birds and the color of the sea. Some think a crystal sunstone helped them on cloudy days, but that is debated.
Tuesday is named for the god Tyr, Wednesday for Odin and Thursday for Thor. Friday is named for Frigg or Freyja.
The first bitcoin block, made January 3, 2009, has a headline from The Times in it: Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.
Only 21 million bitcoin will ever exist. The reward for making new ones is cut in half about every four years, most recently in April 2024.
On May 22, 2010 a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, the first well-known purchase made with bitcoin.
In October 2009 the first published bitcoin price was set from the cost of the electricity used to make one: about 1,309 bitcoin for a dollar.
Bitcoin first reached $1 in February 2011, $1,000 in November 2013, about $20,000 in December 2017 and $100,000 in December 2024.
In its day the Mt. Gox exchange handled most of the world's bitcoin trades. It collapsed in February 2014 with about 850,000 bitcoin missing.
Satoshi Nakamoto, the unknown creator of bitcoin, is estimated to hold about one million bitcoin that has never moved.
The U.S. approved the first spot bitcoin ETFs on January 10, 2024.
Ethereum was proposed by Vitalik Buterin in late 2013, when he was 19, and went live on July 30, 2015.
In 2016 a hack of a project called The DAO led to a split in Ethereum, which is why Ethereum and Ethereum Classic both exist.
On September 15, 2022 Ethereum switched from mining to staking, cutting its energy use by more than 99.9%.
All 100 billion XRP were created at the start. None are mined, and Ripple holds a large share of them.
The XRP Ledger went live in 2012 and settles a payment in about 3 to 5 seconds.
Dogecoin was made in December 2013 as a joke, using the Shiba Inu dog meme as its face.
Litecoin was created in 2011 by Charlie Lee. It makes a block about every 2.5 minutes, four times faster than bitcoin, and caps at 84 million coins.
Binance sold its own token, BNB, to the public in July 2017, the same year the exchange was founded.
Coinbase went public by direct listing on Nasdaq on April 14, 2021, the first big crypto exchange to do it.
Kraken, one of the oldest crypto exchanges still running, was founded in 2011.
On the island of Yap people used giant stone discs as money and tracked who owned them by memory, without moving them. That is a lot like a blockchain ledger.
The New York Stock Exchange traces back to May 17, 1792, when 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement under a tree on Wall Street.
The Dutch East India Company sold the first shares to the public in Amsterdam in 1602.
On October 19, 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% in one day, its biggest one-day percentage drop ever.
After the 1929 crash the Dow did not get back to its 1929 high until November 1954.
The Nasdaq, which opened on February 8, 1971, was the world's first electronic stock market.
After the 1987 crash U.S. exchanges added circuit breakers that pause trading. They fired four times in two weeks in March 2020.
One-letter stock tickers are prized: F is Ford and T is AT&T.
Japan's Nikkei 225 peaked on December 29, 1989 and took until February 2024, over 34 years, to climb back above that high.
On April 20, 2020 the U.S. oil price went below zero for the first time ever, closing near minus $37 a barrel.
The foreign exchange market is the biggest market on Earth, trading about $7.5 trillion a day in 2022.
The U.S. Federal Reserve was created on December 23, 1913.
The U.S. government issued greenbacks, paper money not backed by gold or silver coin, to help pay for the Civil War.
The euro began as an electronic currency in 1999. Euro notes and coins only arrived on January 1, 2002.
In 2009 Zimbabwe printed a 100 trillion dollar note during a hyperinflation.
The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to raise money for a war with France.
